title: Light from the Sun is eight minutes old
body: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to travel the roughly 150 million kilometres to Earth. If the Sun vanished, we wouldn't know for over eight minutes.

title: Octopuses have three hearts
body: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and a third pumps it to the rest of the body. Their blood is blue because it uses a copper-based molecule, hemocyanin, to carry oxygen.

title: Venus spins backwards
body: Venus rotates in the opposite direction to most planets, and so slowly that a day on Venus (one full rotation) lasts longer than its year.

title: Water expands when it freezes
body: Most substances shrink as they solidify, but water expands by about 9%. That's why ice floats, which keeps lakes from freezing solid and lets life survive beneath.

title: You share DNA with bananas
body: Many basic genes that run cell life are shared across living things. A large share of human genes have recognizable counterparts in plants like bananas, a sign of common ancestry.

title: Honey doesn't spoil
body: Honey is low in water and slightly acidic, and bees add an enzyme that produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide. Sealed properly, it can stay edible for an extremely long time.

title: Atoms are mostly empty space
body: If an atom's nucleus were the size of a marble in the middle of a football stadium, the electrons would be zipping around the outer stands. Nearly all of an atom's mass sits in that tiny nucleus.

title: Trees talk through fungi
body: Underground fungal networks connect the roots of many trees. Through them, trees can exchange water, sugars and chemical signals, sometimes nicknamed the "wood wide web".

title: A teaspoon of neutron star
body: Neutron stars are the collapsed cores of giant stars. Their matter is so dense that a teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes on Earth.

title: Why the sky is blue
body: Air molecules scatter short blue wavelengths of sunlight much more than long red ones. That scattered blue light reaches your eyes from every direction, so the whole sky looks blue.

title: Sharks are older than trees
body: The earliest sharks appeared around 400 million years ago, while the first true trees appeared a little later, around 385 million years ago.

title: The Moon is drifting away
body: Tidal interactions slowly push the Moon outward by about 3.8 centimetres a year, roughly the speed your fingernails grow. Earth's day is lengthening very slightly as a result.

title: Cleopatra lived closer to the Moon landing than to the pyramids
body: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BC. Cleopatra lived around 30 BC, about 2,500 years later, and less than 2,000 years before Apollo 11.

title: Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire
body: Teaching at Oxford existed by 1096. The Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325, more than two centuries later.

title: The shortest war in history
body: The Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 lasted somewhere between 38 and 45 minutes before the Sultan's forces surrendered.

title: The printing press changed everything
body: Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg developed a movable-type printing press in Europe. Books became far cheaper, literacy spread, and ideas could travel faster than ever.

title: Ancient Romans used concrete that heals itself
body: Roman concrete contained lime fragments that react with water seeping into cracks, forming new minerals that seal them. Some Roman harbours have survived two thousand years of seawater.

title: The Great Library wasn't burned in one day
body: The Library of Alexandria declined over centuries through budget cuts, political purges and several fires, rather than disappearing in a single dramatic blaze.

title: Paper money started in China
body: During the Song dynasty, around the 11th century, China began issuing government paper money, centuries before it became common in Europe.

title: Napoleon wasn't especially short
body: Napoleon was about 1.69 m, average for a Frenchman of his time. The myth came partly from confusion between French and English inches and from British cartoons.

title: The Berlin Wall fell by accident
body: On 9 November 1989, an East German spokesman mistakenly announced that new travel rules took effect immediately. Crowds rushed the checkpoints, and guards eventually opened the gates.

title: Vikings reached North America first
body: Around the year 1000, Norse explorers led by Leif Erikson reached Newfoundland. Archaeologists found their settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows, nearly 500 years before Columbus.

title: Your body replaces its cells constantly
body: Different cells renew at different speeds: some gut lining cells last only days, skin cells a few weeks, red blood cells about four months, while many neurons last a lifetime.

title: The gut has its own nervous system
body: The enteric nervous system, with hundreds of millions of neurons, lines the digestive tract. It's sometimes called the "second brain" because it can work semi-independently.

title: Muscle protects you as you age
body: After about age 30, people tend to lose muscle mass gradually. Strength training is one of the best ways to slow that loss and stay independent later in life.

title: Daylight sets your body clock
body: Bright light in the morning helps reset your internal 24-hour rhythm, making it easier to feel alert in the day and sleepy at night.

title: Dehydration hits focus quickly
body: Even mild dehydration, around 1–2% of body weight, has been linked to lower concentration and more fatigue. Thirst is a late signal, so sip regularly.

title: Laughing is a mini workout
body: Laughter briefly raises heart rate and breathing, then leaves muscles relaxed. Shared laughter also strengthens social bonds.

title: The spotlight effect
body: We overestimate how much others notice our appearance and mistakes. In studies, people wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed twice as many people noticed it as actually did.

title: The Zeigarnik effect
body: Unfinished tasks stay on our minds more than finished ones. That's why cliffhangers are so effective and why writing down open loops helps you relax.

title: The Dunning–Kruger effect
body: People with low skill in an area often overestimate their ability, partly because the knowledge needed to perform well is the same knowledge needed to judge performance.

title: The mere exposure effect
body: The more often we see something, the more we tend to like it, even without noticing. Familiarity breeds fondness, which is why ads repeat.

title: The Pygmalion effect
body: When teachers were led to expect certain students to bloom, those students often performed better. Expectations can shape performance.

title: Choice overload
body: In a famous jam-tasting study, shoppers offered 24 flavours were less likely to buy than those offered 6. Too many options can paralyse decisions.

title: Your brain is a prediction machine
body: The brain constantly guesses what will happen next and compares the guess with what the senses report. Surprises, the prediction errors, are what grab your attention.

title: The rule of 72
body: Divide 72 by an annual interest rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double. At 6% a year, it doubles in about 12 years.

title: Inflation silently shrinks cash
body: At 3% inflation, prices roughly double in 24 years. Money left in a no-interest account loses about half its buying power over that time.

title: The first coins came from Lydia
body: The kingdom of Lydia, in today's Turkey, minted some of the first known coins around the 7th century BC from electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver.

title: Most money is digital
body: In modern economies, physical cash makes up only a small fraction of the money supply. Most money exists as bank account balances created through lending.

title: Lifestyle creep
body: As income rises, spending tends to rise with it, so people earning more can feel just as stretched. Saving a fixed share of each raise prevents this.

title: The Pomodoro Technique
body: Developed by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s, it uses 25-minute work sprints followed by 5-minute breaks. The name comes from his tomato-shaped kitchen timer.

title: The Eisenhower matrix
body: Sort tasks by urgent and important into four boxes: do now, schedule, delegate, delete. It's named after U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower's approach to priorities.

title: Decision fatigue
body: Making many decisions in a row can wear down the quality of later choices. Routines, like a fixed breakfast or outfit, save mental energy for decisions that matter.

title: Context switching has a cost
body: Research on task switching shows that jumping between tasks slows you down and increases errors, because your brain has to reload the rules for each task.

title: The incubation effect
body: Stepping away from a problem, especially to do something undemanding like showering or walking, often helps the solution pop up later.

title: Constraints boost creativity
body: Dr. Seuss wrote Green Eggs and Ham on a bet that he couldn't write a book using only 50 different words. Limits force unusual solutions.

title: Edison's many failures
body: Thomas Edison's lab tested thousands of materials for the light bulb filament. Breakthroughs often come from systematic trial and error, not flashes of genius.

title: Listening beats talking
body: People tend to like those who ask follow-up questions. In studies of conversations, asking more questions, especially follow-ups, made people more likeable.

title: The 7-38-55 myth
body: The claim that words carry only 7% of meaning comes from narrow experiments about inconsistent messages of feeling. It doesn't apply to everyday conversation.

title: There are about 7,000 languages
body: Roughly 7,000 languages are spoken today, but about 40% are endangered, many with fewer than a thousand speakers.

title: Dunbar's number
body: Anthropologist Robin Dunbar suggested humans can maintain about 150 stable relationships, with smaller inner circles of around 5 close and 15 good friends.

title: Friendship takes time
body: One study estimated it takes around 50 hours together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, and around 200 hours to become close friends.

title: Hugs release oxytocin
body: Warm physical contact like hugging triggers the release of oxytocin, a hormone linked to bonding, trust and lower stress.

title: Your mind wanders half the time
body: A large smartphone study found people's minds were wandering nearly 47% of their waking hours, and they tended to be less happy when it did.

title: Box breathing
body: Inhale for four seconds, hold for four, exhale for four, hold for four. This simple pattern is used by athletes and soldiers to calm down under pressure.

title: Nature lowers stress
body: Spending around two hours a week in nature, in one go or spread out, has been associated with better health and wellbeing in large surveys.

title: The first web page
body: Tim Berners-Lee published the first website at CERN in 1991. It explained what the World Wide Web was and how to use it.

title: Network effects
body: Some products become more valuable as more people use them, like phones or social networks. This creates winner-take-most markets.

title: Most famous startups pivoted
body: Many well-known companies started as something else: Slack began as a game company, and YouTube was briefly a video dating site.

title: Psychological safety
body: Google's Project Aristotle found that the most important factor in effective teams was psychological safety: members felt safe to take risks and speak up.

title: Two-pizza teams
body: Amazon popularized the idea that a team should be small enough to be fed by two pizzas. Smaller teams communicate faster and own their work.

title: The 10,000-hour rule is a simplification
body: The research behind it showed elite performers had practised a lot, but the number varies widely by field. Quality of practice matters as much as quantity.

title: Weak ties find jobs
body: Sociologist Mark Granovetter found people often get jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends, because acquaintances move in different circles.

title: The ship of Theseus
body: If every plank of a ship is replaced over time, is it still the same ship? This ancient puzzle asks what makes something keep its identity through change.

title: Occam's razor
body: When two explanations fit the facts equally well, prefer the one with fewer assumptions. It's named after the 14th-century friar William of Ockham.

title: The trolley problem
body: Would you pull a lever to divert a runaway trolley so it kills one person instead of five? The puzzle explores how we weigh outcomes against actions.
